common_name: Marydel Azalea (Fragrant White Pink-Edged Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; spreads slowly by stolons into a broad colony rather than staying a single tidy shrub.

directions: Marydel is a natural-origin hybrid between two southeastern native azaleas, coast azalea (R. atlanticum) and pinxterbloom azalea (R. periclymenoides), first found growing wild near the Maryland-Delaware border for which it is named. Its funnel-shaped flowers open white with a deep pink-flushed tube and pink-edged petals in mid-to-late spring, carrying a strong, sweet fragrance typical of both parent species. The low, slowly stoloniferous shrub spreads into an open colony rather than a single upright stem, making it well suited to a partly shaded woodland edge or naturalized native shrub border. Give it consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil and dappled shade, mirroring the coastal-plain woodlands where its parent species both occur.

common_name: Camp's Red Cumberland Azalea (Compact Bright Red Selection)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; chosen for flower color noticeably more saturated red than typical wild Cumberland azalea seedlings.

directions: Camp's Red is a compact, low-growing selection of the Cumberland (Bakeri) azalea, prized for bright, saturated red flowers that stand out among the more variable orange-red tones of typical wild seedlings. Like the species, it blooms in early to midsummer after the leaves have fully expanded, later than most spring-flowering native azaleas, extending the native azalea season. Its dwarf, loose, airy 18-24 inch habit fits well at the front of a woodland border or native shrub bed where larger azaleas would overwhelm the space. Native to the Cumberland Plateau and adjacent mountains of Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and Alabama, it prefers moist, acidic, well-drained soil in dappled shade rather than deep shade or exposed full sun.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Aromi Sunny Side-Up Azalea (Fragrant Golden-Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; grows considerably larger over time than many named native-hybrid azaleas.

directions: Aromi Sunny Side-Up is one of Dr. Eugene and Jane Aromi's Mobile, Alabama-bred deciduous azalea hybrids, developed by crossing Exbury hybrids with southern native azalea species for heat tolerance. It produces abundant, rounded clusters of solid yellow flowers with an orange-gold flare on the upper petals in early spring, backed by a notably strong, pleasant fragrance. The shrub grows larger over time than many compact native hybrids, eventually forming an upright large shrub well suited to the back of a woodland border. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade for best performance through hot, humid Gulf South summers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Millennium Swamp Azalea (Fragrant Dark Pink Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; do not allow the shallow root zone to dry out during establishment.

directions: Millennium is a selection of swamp azalea chosen for velvety red flower buds that open into dark pink, clove-scented flower clusters in late May and June, a deeper color than the typically white to pale pink wild species. Deadheading spent blooms can help extend the flowering display further into summer. Like the species, it tolerates wet, clay, and periodically flooded soils better than almost any other native azalea, reflecting its origin in swamps and stream margins of the eastern United States, and it draws butterflies and hummingbirds while in bloom. Site it at a woodland edge or rain garden margin in moist to wet, acidic soil with partial shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Apricot Glow Plumleaf Azalea (Orange-Flowered Midsummer Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil at a shaded ravine or woodland edge; selected for orange flower tone and an upright habit with rounded foliage.

directions: Apricot Glow is a selected form of plumleaf azalea bearing orange flowers in midsummer on an upright-growing shrub with rounded foliage, distinguishing it from the more common red-toned wild seedlings of the species. Like the species, it withholds its display until July and August, long after other rhododendrons and azaleas have finished blooming, extending the native azalea season into the heat of summer and providing nectar for hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies. Plumleaf azalea is naturally confined to a handful of shaded ravines along the Chattahoochee River Valley of Georgia and Alabama, so give Apricot Glow consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil and dappled woodland shade rather than open sun. Mulch heavily to conserve the soil moisture this late-blooming species depends on through summer heat.
sources: Journal of the American Rhododendron Society
